router.subject: Psychology
router.title: Why We Put Things Off
paragraphs: Almost everyone has delayed an important task, such as studying for an exam, even when they knew the delay would cause trouble later. This habit is called procrastination. It is often blamed on laziness or poor time management, but many psychologists now believe that the real cause lies elsewhere.

According to this view, procrastination is mainly a way of managing emotions. A difficult task can produce unpleasant feelings, including boredom, anxiety, and doubt about one's own ability. Turning to something more enjoyable, like watching videos, brings immediate relief. The human mind also tends to value rewards that come now more than rewards that come later, so the comfort of the present moment easily outweighs a distant deadline. The relief is temporary, however, and the unfinished work usually returns with added stress and guilt.

Understanding this cycle suggests practical remedies. Dividing a large project into small steps makes the first step less frightening, and removing distractions, for example by switching off a phone, reduces temptation. Surprisingly, being kind to oneself also seems to help. In one study, students who forgave themselves for delaying their preparation for an exam procrastinated less before the next one. Harsh self-criticism, by contrast, tends to increase the negative feelings that led to the delay in the first place.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Methods that teachers use to help students meet their deadlines
The emotional roots of delaying tasks and ways to reduce it
Reasons that time management skills are declining among students
The harmful effects of stress and guilt on exam results
questions.why: Paragraph 2 explains procrastination as 'a way of managing emotions'; paragraph 3 gives 'practical remedies'.

questions.q: According to the passage, why do people turn to enjoyable activities instead of a difficult task?
options: They have forgotten when the task is due.
They believe the task is not really important.
They want quick relief from unpleasant feelings.
They produce better work when a deadline is close.
questions.why: A difficult task produces 'unpleasant feelings', and turning to something enjoyable 'brings immediate relief'.

questions.q: The word "remedies" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: solutions
warnings
questions
experiments
questions.why: A remedy is a cure or solution; the paragraph goes on to list ways of dealing with the problem.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a way to reduce procrastination?
options: Breaking a project into smaller parts
Turning off a phone
Forgiving oneself for earlier delays
Promising oneself a reward
questions.why: Paragraph 3 mentions small steps, switching off a phone and self-forgiveness. Rewards appear only in paragraph 2, as part of the cause.

questions.q: What can be inferred about students who criticize themselves severely for procrastinating?
options: They usually begin their work earlier the next time.
They are likely to go on delaying their work.
They forget deadlines more often than other students.
They feel less anxious when exams come.
questions.why: 'Harsh self-criticism... tends to increase the negative feelings that led to the delay in the first place', so the delay is likely to continue.

upper.subject: Environmental science
upper.title: Reading the Rings
paragraphs: In regions with distinct seasons, a tree adds a new layer of wood beneath its bark every year. Rapid growth in spring produces pale wood, while slower growth late in the summer leaves a thin, dark band. Together, the two form one annual ring, so counting the rings of a trunk reveals the tree's age. The rings record far more than age, however.

Because trees grow more in favorable years, a wide ring generally indicates plentiful rain and a narrow one drought or cold. Trees throughout a region therefore share a similar sequence of wide and narrow rings. By matching the pattern in a living tree with the overlapping pattern in older wood, such as beams from historic buildings, researchers can extend the record back thousands of years. This technique has allowed archaeologists to date ancient wooden structures to the very year their timber was cut, and it has given climate scientists a year-by-year account of past droughts.

The method is not without shortcomings. Many tropical trees, which grow throughout the year, form no clear annual rings. Moreover, a narrow ring is ambiguous: it may reflect a dry year, but an insect attack or the shade of a taller neighbor can stunt growth as well. For this reason, scientists avoid drawing conclusions from a single tree and compare samples from many trees instead.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How certain trees manage to survive long periods of drought
Why trees in tropical regions grow faster than those elsewhere
How the rings in wood supply information about the past
Which methods archaeologists use to preserve very old timber
questions.why: The passage explains how rings form, what they record ('far more than age') and the limits of the method.

questions.q: According to the passage, what makes it possible to extend the tree-ring record beyond the life of a living tree?
options: Patterns in older wood overlap with those in living trees.
Tropical trees live much longer than trees in other regions.
The dark bands in very old wood are easier to count.
Historic buildings contain written records of past weather.
questions.why: 'By matching the pattern in a living tree with the overlapping pattern in older wood... researchers can extend the record back thousands of years.'

questions.q: The word "ambiguous" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: rare
damaged
misplaced
unclear
questions.why: Something ambiguous can be understood in more than one way; a narrow ring may have several causes.

questions.q: What can be inferred about a tree that shows one very narrow ring?
options: It was growing in a tropical region.
That tree alone cannot reveal the cause.
It was cut down during that year.
It must have lived through a severe drought.
questions.why: A narrow ring may mean a dry year, insects or shade, so scientists 'avoid drawing conclusions from a single tree'.

questions.q: Why does the author mention beams from historic buildings?
options: To show that old buildings were stronger than modern ones
To explain why narrow rings are common in old wood
To give an example of older wood that researchers use
To argue that historic buildings deserve better protection
questions.why: The beams follow 'such as': they are an example of the 'older wood' whose pattern is matched with living trees.

router.subject: Zoology
router.script: OK, let's start with a puzzle. How does an animal catch a tiny flying insect in complete darkness? Bats do it hundreds of times a night. And no, it's not because they have amazing eyes. By the way, bats aren't blind. That's a myth. But in the dark, they rely on something else, called echolocation. Here's how it works. As a bat flies, it sends out very short, very high calls. Most of them are too high for human ears, so to us the night seems quiet. When a call hits an object, say, a moth, an echo bounces back. The bat's brain measures how long that echo took to return. A quick echo means the moth is close. A slower one means it's farther away. And the bat doesn't call at a steady rate. When it's just searching, it might call ten or twenty times a second. But as it closes in on an insect, the calls come faster and faster, up to two hundred a second. Scientists actually call this the feeding buzz. So the bat gets more and more detail exactly when it needs it. Now, the insects aren't helpless. Some moths have ears that can pick up bat calls, and when they hear one, they dive toward the ground. So next time, we'll look at this contest between the hunter and the hunted.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
options: Why bats are active only at night
How bats use sound to find their prey
How moths protect themselves from birds

questions.why: The professor explains echolocation: calls, echoes and what the bat learns from them.

router.subject: Economics
router.script: Let's begin with a simple question. Why do countries trade at all? Why doesn't each country just make everything it needs? Well, part of the answer is obvious. Bananas grow easily in Ecuador. They don't grow easily in Norway. So Norway buys bananas, and it sells things like fish and oil. But here's the less obvious part. Trade can help both sides even when one country is better at making everything. This idea goes back to David Ricardo, an English economist writing in the early eighteen hundreds. Economists call it comparative advantage. Let me give you an everyday example. Imagine a doctor who also happens to type faster than her assistant. Should she do her own typing? No. Every hour she spends typing is an hour she isn't seeing patients, and that's where she's most valuable. So she hires the assistant, and they're both better off. Countries work the same way. A country gains by concentrating on what it does best, compared with its other options, and trading for the rest. Now, I'm not saying trade is painless. When cheaper imports arrive, some local factories close, and those workers pay a real price. But for the economy as a whole, most economists agree that specializing and trading leaves countries richer than doing everything alone.

options: Why some countries produce more than others

upper.subject: Engineering
upper.script: Here's something that ought to embarrass modern engineers a little. A concrete sea wall built today may start crumbling within fifty years. Yet Roman harbors have sat in salt water for two thousand years, and the Pantheon's concrete dome in Rome is still standing after nearly nineteen centuries. So what did the Romans know that we don't? Well, their recipe was different. Instead of modern cement, they mixed lime with volcanic ash. And in sea water, something remarkable happens. The water seeps in and reacts with the ash, and over time new crystals grow inside the concrete. In other words, the very thing that destroys our concrete made theirs stronger. There's a second clue. Roman concrete is full of tiny white lumps of lime. For years, people wrote these off as sloppy mixing. But recent research suggests they act as a repair kit. When a crack opens and rainwater gets in, it dissolves some of that lime, which then hardens again and seals the crack. Now, before you get carried away, Roman concrete isn't better across the board. It's weaker than ours under heavy loads, and it sets slowly. You couldn't build a skyscraper with it. Still, cement production is a major source of carbon emissions, so a concrete that repairs itself and lasts for centuries is well worth a second look.

upper.subject: Sociology
upper.script: Think about the last time you heard about a job opening, or an apartment, or even a good film. Who told you? Your best friend? Possibly. But there's a fair chance it was someone you barely know. Back in nineteen seventy-three, the sociologist Mark Granovetter published a paper with a wonderfully paradoxical title, The Strength of Weak Ties. By strong ties, he meant close friends and family. Weak ties are acquaintances: an old classmate, a neighbor you nod to. Granovetter had asked people near Boston how they'd found their jobs. And of those who'd heard through a personal contact, most said it was someone they saw only occasionally or rarely. Not a close friend. Why would that be? Well, your close friends know one another. They read the same things and hear the same news, so what they tell you is, more often than not, something you already know. An acquaintance, on the other hand, moves in different circles. She's a bridge to information that would never reach you otherwise. Now, I'm not suggesting close friends don't matter. They're the ones who'll help you move house or sit with you when things go wrong. Weak ties won't do that. But when it comes to fresh information, it's the people at the edge of your social world who tend to deliver.

questions.why: 'When it comes to fresh information, it's the people at the edge of your social world who tend to deliver.'

questions.why: 'Most said it was someone they saw only occasionally or rarely. Not a close friend.'

To show that strong ties have their own value
questions.why: 'I'm not suggesting close friends don't matter. They're the ones who'll help you move house'; 'weak ties won't do that'.

email.model:

I am writing about order number 60731, which I placed on your website on August 18. I ordered the fifth edition of my biology textbook, but the package that arrived yesterday contained the third edition. The covers look similar, but the chapters and exercises are different.

professor.name: Dr. Nakamura
professor.post: This week we are examining how the workplace has changed. In recent years, millions of office employees have started working from home, and many companies have found that the work still gets done. Some firms have since told their staff that they never need to return to the office, while others have called everyone back. I would like to hear your view. Should companies allow employees to work from home permanently? Why or why not?

students.name: Yuki
students.post: I think companies should allow it. My mother used to spend almost three hours a day traveling to and from her office. Now she works from home, and she uses that time to exercise and to have dinner with us. She says she is less tired and gets more done, so both she and her employer benefit.

students.name: Mateus
students.post: I disagree. When everyone works at home all the time, new employees have nobody to learn from. In my first part-time job, I learned the most by watching experienced coworkers and asking quick questions at the next desk. That kind of learning does not happen in a video meeting.

discussion.model: In my view, companies should let employees work from home permanently if they wish, but they should not close their offices completely. I agree with Yuki that avoiding a long commute gives people more time and energy. However, Mateus makes a fair point about new staff, who need contact with experienced colleagues. I would add an idea that neither of them mentioned: permanent remote work allows a company to hire talented people who live far from its office, including parents of young children and people with disabilities who find daily travel difficult. This makes the workforce more diverse and gives the company a wider choice of candidates. To deal with the problem Mateus describes, firms could bring teams together for a few days each month for training and planning. In this way, employees keep their freedom, and the company keeps its team spirit.

interview.scenario: You have agreed to take part in a research study about cooking and eating habits. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

questions.q: Thank you for taking part today. Let's start with something simple. Think about the last meal that you cooked or helped to cook. What was it, and who did you make it for?
questions.model: The last meal I cooked was a simple fried rice, which I made on Sunday evening for my two roommates. We had some rice left from the day before, so I added eggs, carrots, green onions, and a little soy sauce. It took only about fifteen minutes. I chose it because it is cheap and fast, and because I did not want to waste the leftover rice. My roommates said it was delicious, although I think they were just being polite, since I put in too much salt. Anyway, we ate together at the kitchen table and talked for an hour, which was the best part.

questions.q: Thanks. Now let's talk about your routine. Some people like to cook at home most days, while others prefer to eat out or order food. Which do you prefer, and why?
questions.model: I prefer cooking at home on most days. The main reason is money: as a student, I cannot afford to eat in restaurants very often, and a home-cooked meal costs less than half as much. Another reason is that I know exactly what is in my food, so I can use more vegetables and less oil. Cooking also helps me relax after a long day of classes. Of course, I still enjoy eating out with friends once or twice a month, especially when we want to try food from another country. But for everyday meals, my own kitchen is the better choice.

questions.q: Now I'd like to hear your opinion. Some people think that eating meals together as a family is less important now than it was in the past, because everyone is so busy. Do you agree with this view? Why or why not?
questions.model: No, I don't agree. I think eating together is more important now exactly because everyone is so busy. During the day, the people in a family are in different places, and in the evening they often look at their own screens. A shared meal may be the only time when they really talk to each other. In my family, dinner was the moment when my parents found out what was happening at school, and when my sister and I heard their stories from work. It does not have to happen every day, and the food does not have to be special. Even two or three meals a week can keep a family close.

questions.q: Here is my final question. Do you think schools should teach all students how to cook basic meals? Why or why not?
questions.model: Yes, I believe schools should teach every student to cook a few basic meals. Cooking is a life skill, just like managing money, and not all children can learn it at home, because many parents work long hours. Students who know how to prepare simple dishes will be able to eat well and save money when they live alone for the first time. Cooking classes are also a practical way to learn about other subjects, for example measuring in mathematics or how heat changes food in science. The lessons would not need much time. One hour a week for a single school year would probably be enough to give young people confidence in the kitchen.
